theme: The covenant lawsuit; seek the LORD and live
readingInstruction: Read Amos 3:1-5:27. These chapters contain three “Hear this word” sermons against Israel, with famous calls to seek the LORD and to let justice roll down. Look for what God says about worship.
settingTheScene: Having announced judgment, Amos now explains why. These chapters are made up of three sermons, each beginning with “Hear this word.” They accuse Israel of oppression and complacency, and of a worship that was lavish but empty. In the middle, there are calls to repentance. The language is vivid and sharp, and includes some of the most quoted lines in the prophets.
observation: “You only have I known of all the families of the earth; therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities” (3:2).
“Do two walk together, unless they have agreed to meet?” (3:3).
“For the Lord GOD does nothing without revealing his secret to his servants the prophets” (3:7).
“The lion has roared; who will not fear? The Lord GOD has spoken; who can but prophesy?” (3:8).
“Hear this word, you cows of Bashan, who are on the mountain of Samaria, who oppress the poor” (4:1).
“Yet you did not return to me, declares the LORD” (4:6, 8, 9, 10, 11).
“Seek me and live” (5:4). “Seek good, and not evil, that you may live” (5:14).
“I hate, I despise your feasts, and I take no delight in your solemn assemblies… But let justice roll down like waters, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream” (5:21, 24).
interpretation:
Chapter 3 opens with one of the most important principles in the prophets: privilege means accountability. “You only have I known… therefore I will punish you.” To be known by God means to be held to his standards. Israel assumed that being God’s people guaranteed protection. Amos says it guarantees accountability.

The series of rhetorical questions in 3:3-8 establishes cause and effect. Do two walk together unless they agree? Does a lion roar without prey? Does a trap spring without bait? Does disaster come to a city unless the LORD has done it? The point is that nothing happens without a cause, and the prophets speak because God has spoken. Amos is not a free agent. “The Lord GOD has spoken; who can but prophesy?”

Chapter 4 addresses the wealthy women of Samaria, whom Amos calls “cows of Bashan,” who oppress the poor and say to their husbands, “Bring, that we may drink!” It then describes God’s attempts to get Israel’s attention: famine, drought, blight, plague, and defeat. After each, the same refrain: “Yet you did not return to me.” It is one of the saddest lines in the Bible. God had been calling through hardship, and they did not listen. The chapter ends with the warning, “Prepare to meet your God, O Israel!”

Chapter 5 begins with a funeral song for Israel and then offers a way out: “Seek me and live.” The alternative is to seek Bethel, Gilgal, and Beersheba, the places of religious activity. God says, “Do not seek Bethel.” The religion of the nation had become a substitute for the LORD himself.

The center of the section is 5:21-24. God says that he hates their feasts. He will not listen to their songs. He rejects their offerings. What he wants is justice and righteousness: “Let justice roll down like waters.” This does not mean that worship is unimportant. It means that worship divorced from justice is an offense. The two belong together.
connection: Martin Luther King Jr. and many others have quoted 5:24 as a call to justice. Jesus echoed the prophets: “Not everyone who says to me, Lord, Lord, will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 7:21). Hebrews 12:25-29 warns against refusing the one who speaks. Revelation 22:17 echoes the call to seek and live. Jesus is the one who “fulfills all righteousness” (Matthew 3:15) and will establish justice (Isaiah 42:1-4).
application:
Ask if your worship and your daily life belong together, or whether there is a gap.

Look back at “Yet you did not return to me.” Is God calling you through something right now?

Pray for justice to roll down like waters in your community, and ask how you can take part.
prayerPrompts: Confess any gap between your praise and your life.
Ask him to let you return when he calls you through hardship.
Ask him to let justice roll in your community.
